name: MinHash and SimHash near-duplicate detection. Aliases: MinHash = min-wise independent permutations, shingling, Broder sketches, LSH banding; SimHash = Charikar's random hyperplane / sign-random-projection LSH. Reference implementations: datasketch (Python), simhash-py, Google's 2007 production simhash, spark-minhash-lsh.
kind: Research result plus a family of algorithms with widely used open-source library implementations. Not a standard and not a browser feature.
maturity: Production, and effectively frozen. MinHash: Broder 1997 (AltaVista). SimHash: Charikar 2002, productionised by Manku, Jain and Das Sarma at Google in 2007 over an 8 billion page repository. Both are textbook algorithms with stable semantics; current research activity is in weighting schemes and in GPU/SIMD acceleration, not in the core.
license: The algorithms are unencumbered (published academic work, no active patent obstacle known for the base constructions). Common implementations are permissive: datasketch is MIT, simhash-py is MIT/BSD-family, Apache DataSketches is Apache-2.0. Permits use in this project. [uncertain] on the precise licence of any specific implementation the project would vendor.
keeps_and_discards: Both discard everything except a fixed-width fingerprint. MinHash keeps a k-permutation sketch (typically 64-256 32-bit or 64-bit minima) of a set of shingles (w-grams of tokens or characters); it therefore preserves an unbiased estimator of Jaccard similarity over the shingle set and discards order, position, structure, and all recoverable content. SimHash keeps a single f-bit vector (f=64 in the Google production setting) formed by summing signed, optionally weighted, hashes of features; it preserves an estimator of cosine similarity over the feature vector and discards the same. Critically for this project: the choice of what becomes a 'shingle' or 'feature' is where all content policy lives, and both papers treat that as out of scope. The classic web-crawling instantiation tokenises the extracted text after HTML stripping, so boilerplate, nav chrome and template text are usually already removed by an upstream extractor -- which is exactly the structure-heuristic step this project refuses. Fed raw serialised markup instead, both fingerprints are dominated by template similarity and near-duplicate recall against *content* collapses, because two unrelated articles on the same CMS share most of their shingles.
structure_preserved: None. This is the defining property and the defining limitation. A fingerprint is a scalar-like object with no nesting, no order, no tabular relation and no shadow-boundary information. Two documents with identical text and completely different DOM structure produce identical MinHash sketches when shingles are drawn from text; the reverse (identical structure, different text) produces distant sketches. If shingles are drawn from a path-tagged token stream -- e.g. hashing the pair (xpath-suffix, token) rather than the token -- structure is partially preserved as a similarity signal, but that is a design choice this project would have to make, not something the literature supplies. For a patricia trie keyed on url:xpath:markdown:content, the natural composition is per-node fingerprints (fingerprint the content field of one trie node) rather than per-page, which preserves structure by keeping it in the key and leaving the fingerprint scalar.
interactive_elements: Not handled. Controls are only visible to these algorithms if they survive into the token stream being shingled. Because the standard pipeline shingles extracted prose, buttons, inputs and their labels are frequently dropped before fingerprinting, so two pages differing only in which form controls are enabled fingerprint as identical. Any interactivity awareness has to be injected by the feature extractor.
interactive_state_fidelity: Zero by construction, and this is the sharpest reason not to use a page-level fingerprint as the dedup key in this project. disabled, checked, selected, expanded and aria-* states are single-token differences. MinHash with 128 permutations over 5-token shingles cannot reliably distinguish documents whose Jaccard similarity is 0.999; the sketch's standard error is roughly 1/sqrt(k), so at k=128 the error is ~8.8%, hundreds of times larger than the signal. SimHash is worse for this purpose: it was explicitly designed so that a small edit changes few bits, and the production threshold k=3 over 64 bits means a page and its state-toggled variant land in the same bucket by design. So a fingerprint answers 'is this substantially the same page' and can never answer 'did the checkbox flip'. If the project uses fingerprints at all, they must sit at a granularity where a state flip is a whole-node change (one trie node = one control), so the state change becomes a node-identity change rather than a sub-threshold perturbation. That is exactly the 'tag plus interactivity' framing paying for itself: put the interactive state into the *key*, not into the fingerprinted *value*.
layout_awareness: None at any pipeline stage. Neither algorithm reads geometry, computed style, or visibility. This makes them constraint-compatible with no_layout_in_the_fold, but also means they cannot distinguish a visible paragraph from a display:none one -- see adversarial_exposure.
javascript_required: No. Both operate on whatever token stream they are handed. They are indifferent to whether that stream came from a static fetch or a live composed DOM. In this project's setting the DOM is already live, so the question does not bear on telemetry; fingerprinting adds no additional network or script activity of its own.
evaluation_method: Manku et al. 2007 evaluated by (a) a correctness/coverage argument for the Hamming Distance Problem solution -- given a query fingerprint, find all stored fingerprints within k bits -- measured as query throughput and memory footprint over 8 billion 64-bit fingerprints, and (b) a manual precision/recall sweep over k, using human judgement of near-duplicate status on sampled pairs. Broder's MinHash is evaluated analytically: the sketch is an unbiased estimator of Jaccard similarity with variance J(1-J)/k, so 'correctness' is a concentration bound rather than a corpus measurement, plus the AltaVista syntactic-clustering experiment over 30 million documents. Henzinger 2006 is the closest thing to an independent head-to-head: it evaluated both families on a large crawl with human-adjudicated pairs and reported that neither is adequate alone on same-site pairs. The important methodological point for this project is that all three establish correctness *against a human notion of 'near-duplicate'*, which is not the notion a delta-store needs. A delta-store needs 'is the stored representation still valid', which is an exact-equality question with an exact oracle (the content hash), not a similarity question.
corpus_size_and_origins: Manku et al.: 8 billion pages from Google's production crawl, circa 2006-2007, origins uncounted but web-scale and English-dominant; the precision/recall sweep itself was over a much smaller human-judged sample (low thousands of pairs) [uncertain on the exact sample size]. Broder 1997: ~30 million documents from a 1996 AltaVista crawl. Henzinger 2006: 1.6 billion pages [uncertain], with a human-judged subsample. Every one of these corpora is 18 to 29 years old, pre-dates single-page applications, shadow DOM, and client-side rendering entirely, and none of them is available for re-running. So the published numbers describe server-rendered 2007 HTML, not the composed-DOM artifacts this project stores. Against the project's own 136 pages from 109 origins, the reach comparison is not favourable in either direction: the literature has scale but no relevance; the project has relevance but no scale.
reported_precision_recall: Manku et al. report that for an 8-billion-page repository, 64-bit simhash with k=3 is 'reasonable', and give a precision-versus-recall curve as a function of k rather than a single operating point; the paper does not publish a single headline precision/recall pair, which is itself worth noting -- the widely cited '64 bits, k=3' is a chosen operating point, not a measured score. [uncertain] on exact percentages at k=3. Henzinger 2006's headline result is the one that matters here: on pairs drawn from the *same* site, precision for both algorithm families is poor -- reported around 0.5 for Broder's shingling and around 0.5 for Charikar's simhash, improving to roughly 0.79 for a combined algorithm that runs Charikar's method and then filters with shingling. [uncertain] on the exact figures. MinHash's Jaccard estimate has no precision/recall at all in isolation; it has a variance J(1-J)/k, giving a standard error of about 8.8% at k=128 and 6.25% at k=256. The project's own 85.5% recall at 98.3% precision is, notably, *better* than Henzinger's same-site figures, which suggests the project's weakest metric is not obviously weak by the standard of the literature -- but the denominators differ so the comparison is indicative only.
independent_oracle: Weak. The oracle in all three studies is human adjudication of 'are these near-duplicates', which shares the ambiguity it is meant to resolve; there is no operator-independent definition of near-duplicate at the boundary. For a delta-store the situation is far better and the project should exploit it: the independent oracle is byte equality of the re-serialised node. A fingerprint claiming two nodes are duplicates can always be checked exactly and cheaply, because the candidate set after LSH banding is small. That converts the whole approach from 'trust the estimator' to 'estimator proposes, exact comparison disposes', which removes the precision problem entirely and leaves only recall as a real metric. This is the single most useful structural observation from this item.
evidence_independence: Mixed, leaning poor. Broder's numbers are AltaVista's own; Manku's are Google's own, on Google's own unpublished corpus, unreproducible by anyone outside. Henzinger 2006 is the closest to independent -- it was written at Google but explicitly as a comparative evaluation of two externally proposed algorithms rather than as a defence of either, and it reports poor absolute numbers, which is the signature of an honest evaluation. Modern library benchmarks (datasketch and similar) are author-run micro-benchmarks measuring throughput, not accuracy. No third party has re-measured either algorithm's near-duplicate accuracy on a modern JavaScript-rendered corpus. [uncertain]
page_archetype_coverage: Not reported, and this is a real gap. None of the three studies breaks results down by article / forum / product / collection / listing / documentation / service. The one structural finding that generalises is Henzinger's same-site versus cross-site split, which is a proxy for the archetype problem: template-dominated pages from a single origin (listings, product pages, forum threads, documentation sets) are precisely where both algorithms degrade, because the shared template dominates the feature vector. Expected ordering, unmeasured: worst on listing and collection pages (near-identical templates, small distinguishing payload), poor on documentation (heavy shared chrome), better on article pages (large distinguishing prose payload), and undefined on service and application pages, which have very little text to shingle at all. Any project-side aggregate over a corpus with the archetype mix unrecorded is uninterpretable for the same reason WCXB's 0.93-to-0.41 spread makes its aggregate uninterpretable.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Structurally script-dependent, contrary to the usual claim that hashing is neutral. Word-level shingling is the standard instantiation and requires whitespace-delimited words, which fails on Chinese, Japanese, Thai and Khmer; on those scripts word shingles either degenerate to whole-sentence tokens (destroying recall) or require a segmenter (importing a locale-specific model, and with it a source of non-determinism and a structure-agnosticism problem). Character n-gram shingling (typically n=4 to n=8 for Latin, n=2 to n=3 for CJK) is script-invariant in principle but the n must be tuned per script, so a single global n is not invariant. RTL scripts are unaffected at the byte level, because logical order is what is stored, but bidi control characters become shingle-bearing tokens and can be used to perturb a fingerprint without visible change. Unicode normalisation form must be pinned (NFC) or the same visible text fingerprints differently across sources. A project claiming script invariance must use fixed-width byte or codepoint n-grams over NFC-normalised text and must say so.
leaks_outward: Nothing, if computed locally. The fingerprint is a pure function of content already in the process. The leak surface appears only if fingerprints are transmitted or shared: a 64-bit simhash of a page is a strong linkage identifier for that page, and a set of simhashes of pages a user visited is close to a browsing history. Publishing or federating fingerprints therefore leaks browsing behaviour even though it leaks no page text. MinHash sketches are worse in one respect: because they are minima of hashed shingles, a sketch supports membership testing against a guessed shingle, so an adversary with a candidate document can confirm you hold it.
mechanism_detectability: Undetectable by the page. Fingerprinting is a read-side computation over data already extracted; it patches nothing, installs no observer the page can see, and adds no timing signal beyond CPU use in the extension or host process. It contributes zero to the detectability budget. This is a genuine advantage over any approach that instruments the page.
countermeasures: Salt the hash function per install so fingerprints are not comparable across users, which removes the cross-user linkage value of a leaked sketch at zero fidelity cost (comparisons within one store are unaffected). Do not export raw fingerprints across a trust boundary. Truncate or bucket fingerprints before any telemetry. Pin the hash function and salt in the store so a re-index is detectable rather than silent. If sketches must be shared, note that neither MinHash nor SimHash is a privacy mechanism -- differentially private sketching is a separate literature and none of these constructions provides any formal guarantee.
measured_fidelity_cost: Per-install salting: zero measured fidelity cost, because it is a relabelling of the hash space and preserves all distances exactly. Truncating a 64-bit simhash to 32 bits: not measured here, but the collision probability at web scale becomes prohibitive by the birthday bound at ~65k documents, so this is a real cost and should not be done. Refusing to export sketches: zero local cost. No study measures the fidelity cost of hardened fingerprinting because there is no accepted hardening to measure; this field is therefore asserted rather than measured, and should be treated as an open item.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented and not representable. A fingerprint of a consent-walled page and a fingerprint of the same page's content are simply different fingerprints with no marker distinguishing them, so a fingerprint-keyed store silently mixes gated and ungated captures and will report the same page as 'changed' when a banner appears or is dismissed. Given that roughly two thirds of top sites present a consent interface, a fingerprint store without an explicit gate-state field in the key will show a large, spurious change rate that looks like real page churn. The trie key must carry gate state; the fingerprint cannot carry it.
determinism: Fully deterministic given a fixed hash function, fixed seed set, fixed shingle definition, fixed tokenisation and fixed Unicode normalisation. All four must be pinned; in practice the tokeniser and the normalisation form are the ones that get left implicit and then drift. There is no randomness at query time -- the 'random' permutations and hyperplanes are pseudo-random from a fixed seed. MinHash and SimHash are therefore among the most reproducible components available, provided the pinning is explicit and versioned.
determinism_across_versions: Stable across browser and platform versions, because there is no browser involvement. The realistic drift sources are all inside the project: a change to the tokeniser, to the shingle width, to the normalisation form, or to the hash implementation (in particular, Python's built-in hash() is salted per process by PYTHONHASHSEED and must never be used) invalidates every stored fingerprint at once. This is a silent global invalidation -- old and new fingerprints compare as maximally distant and everything looks changed. A fingerprint scheme version must be stored alongside the fingerprint and checked on read.
reproducibility: High for the algorithm, near zero for the published evaluations. Any result can be re-obtained from the same bytes with the same parameters indefinitely. But none of the reference corpora (AltaVista 1996, Google 2006-2007, Henzinger's crawl) is available, so the published accuracy figures cannot be re-obtained by anyone, ever. Treat those numbers as historical context, not as a target to hit or a baseline to beat.
failure_modes: Five that matter here. (1) Template domination: on template-heavy origins, similarity is dominated by shared chrome and unrelated pages score as near-duplicates -- Henzinger's same-site precision collapse. (2) Threshold cliff: LSH banding gives an S-curve, so pairs just below the band threshold are missed entirely and no amount of candidate re-ranking recovers them; this is the mechanism behind a recall figure like 85.5% sitting next to a precision figure like 98.3%, since banding is tuned to be conservative. (3) Short-document degeneracy: a node with fewer tokens than the shingle width produces an empty or single-element shingle set, and the estimator is undefined or maximally noisy; in a per-node trie this is the common case, not the rare one, because most trie nodes are short. (4) Seed or parameter drift, silently invalidating the store. (5) Adversarial fingerprint collision: both constructions are non-cryptographic and second-preimage attacks are cheap, so a hostile page can produce a node that fingerprints identically to a previously stored benign node.
failure_visibility: Silent by default, in every one of the five modes. A fingerprint mismatch and a fingerprint match are both plausible-looking outcomes; nothing raises. This is the anti-pattern the project already refuses elsewhere, and it is intrinsic here: an estimator has no error channel. The only way to make it loud is to run the exact comparison behind it, which is affordable at trie-node granularity and turns every false-positive into a detected-and-corrected event and every mismatch into an unambiguous change. The short-document degeneracy case can and should raise explicitly -- if a node has fewer tokens than the shingle width, the correct behaviour is to fall back to exact hashing and record that it did, not to emit a meaningless sketch.
scale_limits: Fingerprint computation is O(document length) with a small constant and is never the bottleneck. Storage is O(number of fingerprinted units): 8 bytes per unit for 64-bit simhash, 512 bytes to 2KB per unit for a 64-to-256-permutation MinHash sketch. The scaling problem is the *lookup*, and it is exactly the failure mode this project is already hitting. Naive all-pairs comparison is O(n^2). Manku's Hamming-distance solution builds several sorted permuted tables and is O(log n) per probe but requires all tables resident; MinHash LSH requires b hash tables of n entries each. Both degrade sharply the moment the index exceeds RAM, and both degrade *before* that as the resident structure exceeds the last-level cache, because every probe is a random access into a structure with no locality. That is a per-insert cost that grows with store size, is spread across cache and TLB misses, and is invisible to a call profiler because it is not attributable to any function -- it is stall cycles inside functions whose call counts are unchanged. This is a strong candidate explanation for the project's 582 to 840 to 1539 ms ingest curve and is testable directly: read hardware cache-miss and page-fault counters, or the process's minor-fault count, at the two store sizes and see whether misses per insert scale like the wall time while call counts stay flat.
delta_cost_model: Per-change cost, when fingerprints are computed per trie node: O(len(node content)) to recompute the changed node's fingerprint, plus O(b) index updates for b LSH bands, plus the amortised cost of the index probe. That probe cost is the term that is *not* constant in store size, which means a naive statement of 'O(delta)' is already false for the index even if it is true for the hash. Changes that fall OUTSIDE the model, named explicitly: (1) any change to shingle width, tokeniser, normalisation form, hash function or seed -- cost O(entire store), and it is silent; (2) a subtree removal, which is one mutation record but invalidates every descendant fingerprint -- cost O(subtree size), not O(1); (3) a change that leaves the fingerprint identical, which costs zero and is therefore *missed*: because SimHash is explicitly designed to be insensitive to small edits, a single-token change inside a large node is exactly the change a page-level fingerprint cannot see, so the delta guarantee is not merely expensive there, it is wrong there; (4) CSS-driven, canvas, video and closed-shadow-root changes, which never reach the token stream at all and so cost nothing and are never detected; (5) declarative shadow DOM present in the initial parse, which is fingerprinted correctly on first read only if the reader traverses it, and never re-fingerprinted if the reader relies on mutation records; (6) index rebalancing and rehashing, which is amortised O(1) per insert on paper and a multi-second stall in practice, attributed to no call.
reanchoring_stability: This is where fingerprints have real, underused value for the project. A content hash is a perfect equality test and a useless identity test: change one byte and identity is lost. A fingerprint degrades gracefully instead -- a node whose text was edited still fingerprints close to its previous self, so a fingerprint is a *re-anchoring signal* of exactly the kind the W3C Web Annotation work concluded was necessary alongside an xpath. Concretely: when an xpath fails to resolve, the set of candidate nodes can be ranked by simhash distance to the stored fingerprint, and the top candidate accepted only if its distance is below a fixed, published threshold and only if it is uniquely below it -- otherwise the re-anchor fails loudly. That construction is bounded, deterministic, and does not contaminate reproducibility, because the threshold is fixed and the tie-break is refusal rather than a heuristic choice. No measured re-anchor rate exists for this construction in the literature; it would have to be measured on the project's own corpus. [uncertain]
adversarial_exposure: Preserves whatever it is fed, and is layout-blind, so it preserves invisible-to-human content with the same weight as visible content. Concretely: text hidden by display:none, clip-path, zero opacity, off-screen positioning or font-size:0 enters the shingle set identically to body text, and a fingerprint therefore certifies as 'unchanged' a page whose visible content changed and whose hidden payload did not, or vice versa. Because both constructions are non-cryptographic and second-preimage-cheap, an adversary who knows the shingle definition can pad a hostile node with chosen tokens until it collides with a stored benign fingerprint, causing a dedup system to *drop* the hostile node as a duplicate -- a suppression attack, not just a false match. Neither algorithm can filter concealment without reading layout, so under no_layout_in_the_fold the fold is structurally more exposed than a heuristic extractor that at least drops display:none subtrees. The honest mitigation is not to filter but to mark: record per-node that concealment could not be assessed, and let the actuator layer, which does read geometry, do the assessment. Silently pretending the fold is clean is the failure to avoid.
provenance_carrying: None at all. A fingerprint is 8 bytes with no origin, no address, no capture time, no shadow depth and no gate state. This is not a defect to be fixed inside the algorithm; it is the reason the fingerprint must never be the key. In this project's design the trie key url:xpath:markdown:content already supplies exactly the provenance a fingerprint lacks, and the correct composition is fingerprint-as-value-under-a-provenanced-key. Stated as a rule: the fingerprint may answer 'has this changed', never 'what is this'.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable in the fixed-point sense -- fingerprinting is one-way and there is no parse step, so serialize -> parse -> serialize is undefined. It does however make a useful oracle-free fidelity metric for something else: if the project's serializer is a fixed point, then fingerprinting the input and the twice-serialised output must yield identical fingerprints, and any drift localises a serializer bug without needing a ground-truth corpus. Escaping policy is upstream and matters: if escaping is not idempotent, fingerprints drift on re-serialisation and every stored node appears changed on the second read.
token_budget_and_ordering: Fingerprints are never emitted to a model and cost zero tokens. Their contribution to the token contract is indirect but real: dedup at ingest is what keeps the same content from occupying a budget slot twice, and near-duplicate suppression across a listing page can be the difference between fitting the distinguishing content of 40 results and fitting 12 near-identical templates. Given that position bias becomes recency-dominant past roughly 50% context fill and that reader accuracy falls sharply as the number of retrieved units grows, suppressing duplicates has a larger effect on effective recall than the token saving alone suggests -- a duplicate is not merely wasted budget, it is a distractor, and the Chroma context-rot work found distractors degrade performance non-uniformly and severely. The ordering implication is that dedup should run before budget allocation, not after truncation.
representation_cost: 8 bytes per 64-bit simhash; 512 bytes at k=64 up to 2KB at k=256 for a MinHash sketch of 64-bit minima. Zero tokens. What is lost per byte saved is total: the fingerprint is not invertible and carries no content, so it can only ever be an index over a store that holds the real bytes elsewhere. Given the storage asymmetry, simhash is the right choice for this project unless set-similarity semantics are specifically needed, since 8 bytes per trie node is negligible while 2KB per trie node is not.
what_could_be_adopted: Three specific mechanisms, in decreasing confidence. (1) Per-trie-node simhash as a change-detection accelerant and, more importantly, as a bounded re-anchoring signal: when an xpath fails, rank surviving candidates by Hamming distance to the stored 64-bit fingerprint and accept only a unique candidate strictly below a fixed published threshold, otherwise fail loudly. This is deterministic, bounded, threshold-published, and refuses rather than guesses, so it does not contaminate reproducibility -- it is the deterministic answer to the 'two xpaths beat one xpath' finding without importing fuzzy matching. (2) The estimator-proposes-exact-disposes pattern: never let a fingerprint be the final word. LSH banding narrows candidates, byte equality decides. This makes precision exactly 1.0 by construction and leaves only recall as a metric to improve, which reframes the project's 85.5%/98.3% pair as a single-number problem. (3) The diagnostic, which is the most immediately valuable thing here: Manku's index structure degrades on random access as it leaves cache and RAM, in a way attributable to no function. Instrumenting cache misses, minor page faults and resident set size per insert at 136 / 250 / 500 pages is a direct test of whether the project's superlinear ingest curve is index locality rather than algorithmic cost. Explicitly NOT adopted: page-level fingerprinting as a dedup key (kills interactive-state fidelity and provenance), and any fingerprint over extractor-cleaned text (imports the structure heuristics the project refuses).
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS with one condition: the algorithms are structure-blind, which is compliant, but the standard *instantiation* shingles boilerplate-stripped prose, which is a structure heuristic. Shingle the raw node content stream, never an extractor's output. Severity: low, fully avoidable. no_layout_in_the_fold -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS. Neither construction reads geometry at any stage. Severity: none. o_delta -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS at node granularity, REJECTED at page granularity. Per-node fingerprinting is O(node); page-level fingerprinting is O(page) per change and additionally *misses* small within-node edits by design, which breaks the guarantee rather than merely costing more. The LSH index probe is not constant in store size and must be declared as an exception. Severity: high if applied at page level. no_mocks -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS. Pure computation, no stubs possible or needed, no subsystem to fake. Severity: none. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS. Fingerprinting requires no page instrumentation, patches nothing, is undetectable, and cannot reach a closed root any more than the reader that feeds it can. Severity: none. Overall verdict: adoptable as-is, at node granularity, as an index and re-anchoring aid, never as an identity key.
governance_signal_handling: No native handling. MinHash and SimHash are post-fetch computations and are indifferent to robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, IETF AIPREF, Web Bot Auth or HTTP 402; all of those must be enforced upstream at the fetcher. One second-order point is worth recording: because a fingerprint is a derived, non-invertible artifact, it is sometimes argued that retaining fingerprints of content one may not retain is permissible. That argument is weak under both the AIPREF direction of travel and GDPR (see below) and should not be relied on. If a fetch was refused or gated, the correct behaviour is to store no fingerprint, not to store a fingerprint of what was not fetched.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 (adopted 7 July 2026, in consultation until 30 October 2026) the regulated act is the collection and retention of personal data, and legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) is the realistic basis, subject to the three cumulative tests. A hash or sketch of personal data is pseudonymised, not anonymised, and remains personal data whenever the underlying content can be re-identified or membership-tested -- which is precisely what a MinHash sketch supports. So fingerprints inherit the lawful basis of the content they summarise and do not launder it. Practical posture for this project: fingerprints are low-volume and non-invertible, so they are the *least* exposed artifact in the store, but they are not exempt; they must fall under the same retention clock and the same erasure path as the node content they index, and an erasure that deletes content while leaving the fingerprint and its provenanced key in place is not an erasure. Special-category data is prohibited in principle and no fingerprinting scheme changes that.
